tagline.text: An island of pure white sandbars spreading two wings toward the sea

items.credit: Bien Orellana Bacarra Jr / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A small island off Palompon on the west coast of Leyte, where long white sandbars stretch from both ends like a bird's wings. With no electricity or shops, this pristine island protects itself by limiting daily visitor numbers, making it ideal for quiet camping and snorkeling.
Kalanggaman Island lies in the Camotes Sea about
1 hour
by bangka west of Palompon, a small port town on Leyte's west coast. The island itself is only about

long and covered in coconut palms and shrubs, but what makes it special are the pure white sandbars stretching far out to sea from both ends. Seen from above, the island looks like a bird spreading its wings, and its name is said to come from "langgam," the Cebuano word for bird.

The sandbars change slightly in length and shape with the tides, and at low tide you can walk out toward what feels like the middle of the sea. The sand is fine white sand made of broken-down coral, and the waters around the island show clear bands of color, from jade in the shallows to deep navy farther out. Coral reefs around the island are full of tropical fish, so you can snorkel right off the beach.

Kalanggaman is an ecotourism zone managed directly by the city of Palompon. The island has no hotels, shops, electricity, or fresh water supply — only a management office, cottages, a camping area, and basic restrooms. To protect the island, the city limits the number of daily visitors and runs an advance reservation system, and in
it raised entrance fees significantly to fund conservation.

It's not the easiest place to reach, but that keeps it far from the crowds of major destinations like Boracay or El Nido. It's especially recommended for travelers who want to spend a whole day on a nearly empty white sandbar, campers who want to pitch a tent and watch the stars for a night, and those who love drone and landscape photography.

blocks.title: Walking to the tip of the sandbar

children.text: The sandbars on either end of the island stretch out for hundreds of meters at low tide. Standing at the end of the thin strip of sand with the sea pressing in from both sides is the heart of the Kalanggaman experience.

The coral reef section along the island's edge is full of clownfish, butterflyfish, sea urchins, and starfish. Starting in the calm water inside the sandbar and gradually moving out to the coral section makes it manageable even for beginners.
On days when drones are permitted, you can capture aerial photos of the whole island looking like a bird. Check the drone rules with the management office first.

Buying an overnight entry pass lets you pitch a tent and spend the night on the island. From the afternoon once the day visitors leave, the whole island practically becomes yours, and at night you can see a sky full of stars and the sunrise at dawn.
The western sandbar of the island faces the Camotes Sea head-on for sunset viewing. On clear days, you can even make out the silhouette of Cebu Island beyond the horizon.

Buying fish, squid, and shellfish at the Palompon market and grilling them yourself on the cottage's grill is a treat of local-style dining. Bring charcoal and tools in advance, or ask your bangka driver.
The management office or tour operators sometimes rent kayaks and paddleboards. Paddling along the sandbar in the calm morning sea is a unique experience.

1 hour 15 minutes

After confirming your advance reservation at the Palompon tourism office (ecotourism office), charter a city-certified bangka. Fares vary by boat size, roughly about
for a 20-seater and about
for a 35-seater — the more people, the lower the cost per person. If you're traveling alone, look for joiner groups through the Palompon tourism office or social media.

March
to

to

During Philippine Holy Week (the week before Easter), the April–
May

summer break, and the year-end holidays, the daily visitor quota fills up quickly, so book several weeks ahead. The low tide when the sandbar is longest varies day to day, so check a tide table and time your arrival on the island accordingly.

Since the island has no hotels and only camping is available, most travelers stay at a small hotel or pension in downtown Palompon (about
per night). Options are limited, so book ahead in peak season, and for a wider choice of accommodation, some stay in Ormoc, about
1 hour
away (about
per night), and head out before dawn. If camping on the island, bring your own tent, mat, and lantern, or check rental availability with the management office.

The island has almost no restaurants or shops, so you need to bring all your food and water. At Palompon's public market, you can buy freshly caught fish, squid, shrimp, and crab cheaply in the early morning, along with charcoal and rice. Leyte's local snacks — binagol, a rice cake made with coconut and taro, and moron, a chocolate-filled sweet — are popular to try or buy at the Ormoc or Tacloban terminals.

Before your trip, confirm your date and group size through Palompon's tourism office or the official booking channel. Arriving without a reservation may mean you can't get on the island if the daily quota is full.

The island has no ATMs or card payments, so bring cash for the entrance fee, bangka fare, and cottage cost. Downtown Palompon has few ATMs, so it's safer to withdraw cash beforehand in Ormoc or Tacloban.
Bring at least 2–3 liters of water per person, and if camping, bring extra water for washing up too.
There's little shade and the sun is very strong, so a hat, sunglasses, a rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen are essential.
The sandbar's tip is longest during the
2-hour
window around low tide, so plan your departure time using a tide table.
Cell signal is often weak or absent on the island, so let family know your itinerary in advance.
Bangka seats get sprayed with sea water, so put electronics and passports in a waterproof bag.

Kalanggaman is a protected area with a daily visitor cap and a reservation system. The entrance fee, capacity, and reservation method can change under Palompon city ordinance, so be sure to check the latest notices before departing.
On the island, you must take all your trash back with you, and single-use plastics are sometimes restricted.
The tip of the sandbar has fast currents where the two sides meet, so don't swim at the very end.
If waves are high or a typhoon signal is raised, the coast guard bans bangka departures, so leave at least a day of buffer in your schedule.
Walking on the coral reef or collecting coral and shells is prohibited.
Staying in the midday sun for long periods carries a high risk of heatstroke, so rest regularly in the cottage's shade and drink water often.
